passage:
In the UKG classroom, Rukmini stood up to read the picture card. "Ell-y-fant," she said.
Laughter rippled across the room. Her cheeks burned and she wanted to shrink into her shoes.
Aparna, the teacher, raised a hand. "Everyone here is still learning words, even me. Let us say it together: el-e-phant." The class repeated it.
One boy near the front was still giggling. Rukmini took a breath. "That is unkind, Rohit."
Rohit stopped and studied his desk. Rukmini said the word again, slowly, and got it right.

qa.q: What word did Rukmini mispronounce?
qa.a: She said "ell-y-fant" for elephant.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: She felt small and embarrassed: her cheeks burned and she wanted to shrink into her shoes.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do when someone keeps laughing?
qa.a: She can say calmly that it is unkind, as she did with Rohit, and keep trying the word.

qa.q: How might Aparna see the laughter in her class?
qa.a: She seems to see it as part of learning together and steps in gently, saying even she is still learning, so no one is singled out.

grounding: The class laughs at a child's mispronounced word; she feels small and hot, a teacher says everyone is learning, and she says that is unkind.

passage:
Monday: Bhavin tripped over his shoelace on the playground and the whole group burst out laughing. Asif laughed loudest, eyes on the others, though his stomach felt a little tight.
Wednesday: Karthik, the teacher, called Asif aside. "When Bhavin fell, you laughed. How would you feel if it was you on the ground?"
Asif looked at his feet. "Sore. And sad."
"Mm," said Karthik, and waited.
Friday: A girl slipped on the wet step and a few children giggled. Asif felt the laugh start in his throat, then swallowed it. "Are you okay?" he asked, holding out his hand.

qa.q: What made Bhavin fall on Monday?
qa.a: He tripped over his shoelace.

qa.q: Why did Asif laugh loudest on Monday even though his stomach felt tight?
qa.a: He wanted to be part of the group, but he also felt a little uneasy, which the tight stomach suggests.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that helped Asif change?
qa.a: He asked Asif to imagine being the one on the ground and then waited quietly, so Asif found the answer himself. 🙂

qa.q: How might Bhavin have felt when the group laughed?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and hurt, since he was on the ground while everyone laughed at him.

grounding: A child laughs at a fallen classmate because everyone does and feels uneasy; an adult asks how he would feel, and he changes over the week.

passage:
"Jamal, stand up and show everyone your sums," said Mr Bilal, holding up the page covered in red crosses.
Jamal walked to the front. His face went hot and his eyes stung. He stared at the carpet while the whole class watched.
At dinner he pushed his rice around the plate.
"What is wrong?" asked Mum.
"The teacher showed my mistakes to everybody."
Mum put down her spoon. "That is not your fault, and I am glad you told me. I will talk to the school so that children can make mistakes and feel safe."
Jamal leaned against her arm.

qa.q: What did the teacher hold up in front of the class?
qa.a: He held up Jamal's page covered in red crosses.

qa.q: How did Jamal feel while standing at the front?
qa.a: He felt hot and wanted to cry, since his face went hot, his eyes stung, and he stared at the carpet.

qa.q: What could Mum do next?
qa.a: She can talk to the school as she promised, so children can make mistakes safely, and keep listening to Jamal.

qa.q: How might Jamal's classmates have felt watching?
qa.a: Some may have felt uncomfortable or afraid that they would be next, since a child was shown up in front of everyone.

grounding: A teacher makes a child show his mistake to the class; he feels hot and wants to cry, tells his parent, and is told it is not his fault.

passage:
At Sameena Khala's house in the kasba, Hafsa carried her glass of orange juice across the room to show the parrot. Her elbow bumped a chair and the juice ran across the mat. She froze, cheeks burning, hand over her mouth.
Noor, her mother, came over. "Accidents happen, Hafsa. Let us clean up together."
She fetched a cloth and gave Hafsa half. Sameena Khala waved from the doorway. "Only juice, beta."
Hafsa wiped slowly, and her breath loosened. On the way home she leaned on her mother's arm. "I thought you would be angry."

qa.q: What did Hafsa spill?
qa.a: She spilled her glass of orange juice.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling after the juice spilled?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and afraid of being in trouble: she froze, her cheeks burned and she covered her mouth.

qa.q: What did Noor's reaction teach Hafsa?
qa.a: That embarrassment passes and mistakes can be mended, because Noor stayed calm and cleaned up alongside her. 🙂

qa.q: How does Sameena Khala see the spill?
qa.a: She seems relaxed about it, since she calls it only juice and waves from the doorway.

grounding: A child spills juice at a guest's house and the parent says accidents happen and cleans up together, so she feels relieved and loved.

passage:
"Yasmin got a gold star again," said his father, Bilal, reading the school sheet. "Why can't you be like your sister?"
Jamal stared at his cereal. His chest went tight. Under the table he kicked Yasmin's chair.
"Stop it!" she said.
"You always get the stars," he muttered.
Later, Bilal found him on the stairs, hugging a cushion.
"That came out wrong," said Bilal. "You draw wonderful animals, and you learn at your own speed. I am sorry."
Jamal sniffed and did not answer, but he let Bilal sit beside him.

qa.q: What did Jamal do under the table?
qa.a: He kicked Yasmin's chair.

qa.q: Why did Jamal kick Yasmin's chair?
qa.a: He felt less loved and angry at his sister after his father compared them, though the comparison was not her fault.

qa.q: What could Bilal do to repair the moment?
qa.a: He can keep valuing Jamal's own strengths, such as his drawing, and avoid comparing the children, as his apology begins to do.

qa.q: How might Yasmin have felt when Jamal kicked her chair?
qa.a: She was probably annoyed and puzzled, since she did nothing wrong and simply got a star.

grounding: A parent asks why the child cannot be like his sister; he feels less loved and angry at her, and the parent later apologises and names his own strengths.

passage:
Note from Devika, class teacher:
For a week Wasim has stopped colouring in class and put his crayons away. On Thursday he said quietly, "Papa says the neighbour's boy can already write his whole name." His jaw was set and he would not look at me. I asked if he could tell Papa how it made him feel. At pick-up I stood nearby. Wasim said, "I feel sad when you say that." His father paused, then apologised and said he would look at Wasim's own progress. The next morning Wasim took out his crayons.

qa.q: What did Wasim stop doing in class for a week?
qa.a: He stopped colouring and put his crayons away.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he said Papa compared him with the neighbour's boy?
qa.a: He was hurt and stubborn: his jaw was set and he would not look at Devika, and he stopped trying.

qa.q: What did Wasim say to his father that helped?
qa.a: He said, "I feel sad when you say that," which told his father honestly what the comparison did, and Papa apologised.

qa.q: How might Papa have seen his comment before Wasim spoke?
qa.a: He may have meant to encourage Wasim and not seen the hurt, since he paused and apologised once he heard it.

grounding: A father compares the child with the neighbour's child; the child feels hurt and stops trying, then says he feels sad, and the father apologises.

passage:
Rafael glanced at Lucia's page. Every colour stayed inside the lines, smooth as glass. His own sun had scribbles over the edge. He slid his arm across the paper.
"Can I see?" asked Javier, the teacher, crouching beside him.
Rafael shook his head. "Hers is neater."
"Wait here." Javier came back with a page from the first week, all big scribbles. "Look how far you have come."
Rafael looked from one page to the other. Now the sun sat mostly inside its circle. Slowly he moved his arm and picked up the yellow crayon again.

qa.q: What did Rafael do with his arm when he saw Lucia's page?
qa.a: He slid his arm across his own paper.

qa.q: Why did Rafael want to hide his colouring?
qa.a: He felt bad because Lucia's page was neater, and he was embarrassed that his sun had scribbles over the edge.

qa.q: How did Javier turn the comparison into something useful?
qa.a: He showed Rafael his own first-week page beside the new one, so Rafael saw his own growth and felt proud enough to carry on. 🙂

qa.q: How might Lucia see her own page in this moment?
qa.a: She is probably just colouring and may not know Rafael is comparing, since nothing in the scene shows her noticing.

grounding: A child compares his colouring with a neighbour's neater page and wants to hide it; the teacher shows how far he has come.

passage:
On the school ground, the racing practice had begun. Shalini ran the whole length of the track and her plaits flew out behind her. Lalremsiami stood at the fence, watching, her hands tight on the wire. She wanted to run like that. A small pinch of jealousy sat next to the wish.
The games teacher came up. "Why not ask her how she does it?"
Lalremsiami walked over. "Can you teach me?"
"Keep your arms bent, like this," said Shalini, showing her. "And push with your toes."
The teacher smiled. "Shalini is fast, and Lalremsiami is the best at catching the ball. Everyone is good at something different."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami ask Shalini?
qa.a: She asked, "Can you teach me?"

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she watched Shalini run?
qa.a: She felt inspired and a little jealous, shown by her tight grip on the wire and her wish to run like that. 😊

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do to get faster?
qa.a: She can practise the tips Shalini gave her, such as bending her arms and pushing with her toes, and ask for more help.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Lalremsiami's request?
qa.a: She seems happy to help, since she shows her straight away and gives clear tips.

grounding: A child sees a classmate run fast and feels inspired and a little jealous; adults help her ask to be taught and note that each child is good at different things.

passage:
At the door of the KG room in the apartment-complex school, Pradeep held on to Mummy's hand as if it were a rope. When she kissed his head and turned to go, he cried loudly and stood rooted.
Chaitanya, the teacher, knelt beside him and took his other hand. "Come, let me show you something." She led him to a shelf of wooden animals. "Which one do you like?"
Pradeep sniffled and pointed to a red tractor. "That."
"Shall we drive it to the mat together?"
He wiped his face on his sleeve and let himself be led, still sniffing, looking back once at the door.

qa.q: What did Pradeep point to on the shelf?
qa.a: He pointed to a red tractor.

qa.q: How was Pradeep feeling when Mummy turned to go, and then when Chaitanya took his hand?
qa.a: He was scared and sad at first, and then a little safe, since he stopped rooting to the spot and followed her to the mat. 🙂

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do that made the school feel friendlier?
qa.a: She stayed warm and steady, took his hand, and offered something interesting to choose and do together.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel leaving while Pradeep cries?
qa.a: She may feel sad and worried herself, since she kissed his head before turning to go and he was crying loudly.

grounding: A child cries as his mother leaves on the first day, then the teacher takes his hand and shows him the toys, and he feels a little safe.

passage:
"Mummy, no, no!" Simran clutched Rekha's kurta with both hands at the school gate.
"I know it is hard, Simran. I will be back after your lunch, when the bell rings. I will wait right here at this gate."
"Stay!"
"Not today. A big hug, then one kiss on the count of three?"
Simran squeezed her tight, sobbing.
Rekha loosened the small fingers gently and walked her to the teacher. "See you after lunch, jaan." She waved once from the gate and did not sneak away.
Simran wailed but watched her go, then let the teacher hold her hand.

qa.q: When did Rekha say she would come back?
qa.a: She said she would be back after Simran's lunch, when the bell rings.

qa.q: How does Simran feel at the gate?
qa.a: She feels deep sadness at the separation: she clutches the kurta with both hands, sobs and begs her mother to stay.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that made parting easier?
qa.a: She said a short kind goodbye, told Simran exactly when she would return, hugged her, and did not sneak away.

qa.q: Why might it have been worse if Rekha lingered or slipped away?
qa.a: Lingering would drag out the pain, and sneaking off might make Simran fear Mummy could vanish, so she would cling harder next time.

grounding: A child holds her mother's kurta and cries at the school gate; the parent says a short kind goodbye, names when she will return and does not sneak away.
